I live and work as a Mixologist in NYC and about once a week, I get asked "What makes a good Bartender??" or an aspiring bartender will say "I keep seeing jobs in NYC that need a bartender with two years experience. What's the difference and why do I need that much experience? I went to insert name bartending school and I have my insert name certification. Doesn't that count for something?

My answer is always the same: It depends.

For NYC, most shot/beer bars/night clubs want a bartender that can sling drinks accurately and quickly - talking T-minus 10 seconds for call drinks, ~20-30 seconds for cocktails, is a wizard with the POS system, and can keep up with the volume and demand of consumers at crunch time, while maintaining their cool.

Sports bars usually have a pair - a guy and a girl - wearing jerseys, or a set of ladies with big smiles and low-cut shirts behind the bar doing their thing to try to encourage guys to buy drinks and tip heavy.

Craft places typically have a neat guy or a set of guys - mustachioed or bearded - that can keep a conversation going about the particular blend of Rye Mash in a certain whiskey and how it compares to something the patron is familiar with, while making a fresh whiskey sour with egg white.

All in all, in a bar in NYC, there's really not a lot of room for amateur hour because mistakes, over pours, or slow movers = lost sales.

But that's just my perspective. What do you Voaters think? What really makes a good bartender?
Discussion Thread: What makes a good bartender?

You're not wrong, personality is chiefly important. But it really depends on the bar and what areas can be weaker and which cant. I work in a multivenue bar-- high end cocktails, craft beer, and some house creations. We have a really nice patio, really expensive food, etc. However at around 10 on the weekends, we cater to our college crowd.

Now, a lot of people can say they tend bar, but not everyone can say they keep their head straight in a bar that gets 3-4 deep consistently.

Hands down, college weekend versus daytime clientele, these are different bar tenders. We've staffed a lot of different people over the past 11 years, I've been there for 6, and I've seen a lot of people come and go.

It's really important to be able to hang during the high end clientele times, because they're sensitive, and want to feel like the most important person there. A great bartender can make everyone feel particularly important, not just taken care of, but special-- while addressing the server well and remembering the calamari before it starts to get cold.

The skills cross over, but night time is less important to worry about the feelings of the crowd. A great bartender here can run 3 cards, pour up to 10 orders, serve the drinks, and doesnt wait at the computer like an idiot with his dick in his hand. That doesn't mean you should be rude to the customers, its just a different priority set based on who keeps which shift. You can get by here by smiling and saying thank you.

The people that keep the day time shifts are the ones that keep the celebrities of the town in the seats, the ones that keep the night time shifts are the ones that keep pulling in the high level sales numbers. Of course, YMMV.

I like to look at it this way: Half the people want someone who knows how to make exactly what they want, to their exact specification, with speed, and gusto! The other half want someone who can keep them entertained, make them laugh, and otherwise distract them from whatever it is that brought them to the bar in the first place. I believe it's a fine balance that needs to be maintained - but a good bartender can hit all points without missing a beat, or breaking a sweat. Ahh, serious bartenders usually will mock the term 'Mixologist' until they actually meet one. The seasoned bartenders usually scoff and I'm normally mocked whenever I come into a new establishment account, or if I introduce myself as "Millesime and this is my Mixology Team." It's almost welcomed honestly - I appreciate it as it lets me know who is who. Then we begin to explain the menu, spirit by spirit, ingredient by ingredient, garnish by garnish, metaphor by metaphor, and why each element makes sense on the palette: why to use a Mole Bitters with an Ancho-Chile rim instead of Angostura and Cayenne or Paprika, why the Juniper and Peppercorn notes are necessary here and not there, and what increasing one thing or another does to a cocktail for a customer.

Bartenders with experience kind of "sense" how to tweak a particular cocktail to match the person ordering it, but don't really know why. Mixologists tend to know why.

And Mixologist is just a title - essentially we're bartenders, but with more in-depth knowledge of cocktails, wines and spirits, and flavors than what is really necessary for a bartender to have. Mixologists study flavor and it's development and match that flavor knowledge up in unique ways. Like, for instance, most bartenders I know wouldn't be able to walk a person through the bouquet of a particular vintage of Veuve or Dom P, let alone why the vanilla notes of a particular cigar paper will work with a 2008 Long Island Chardonnay, but not a 2010.

Sounds like you're a great bartender. I think I understand where you're coming from. "Bartender" signifies that you get paid to stand behind a bar. Other than that, it doesn't really specify much, other than:

  1. you were hired
  2. you haven't been fired
  3. it's a bar

Some people pour beer for a living, and all they will ever pour is beer. For some, it is because that is all their customers come in for, for others, it is a beer destination, where you can come in and expect the person behind that bar to explain, in great detail, everthing about any beer they might put in front of you. But we call them both bartenders.

Some people pour wine for a living. Some pour a few bottles here and there to make their restaurant relevant, some are incredibly pricey and have an incredible report with the wine drinking community. Some of the people that stand behind these bars have studied for years, they have taken rigorous tests, and they are bartenders.

Some bartenders pour cocktails. Some make mostly gin and tonics for law students that just want something quick, simple, and refreshing. Some work in gin and tonic bars in tourist areas of spain, where they hold competitions every year to see who makes the best gin and tonic, who can create an incredible symphony with such simple ingredients and a keen attention to detail. Are these really both bartenders? Are they really in the same category? My friend Jake at the dive bar next store, who pours beers and shots, and Mr. Zaric-- they have the same job?

I usually lean towards yes. Over the years, a very important thing I've noticed that is common amongst all great bartenders is humility. That includes Mr. Zaric, Jeff Meehan, and Jake from next door. There is nothing wrong with trying to explain to someone what it is you do, but a title won't really accomplish that, especially such a tainted one.

My bar gets 3-4 deep often. We sell more than anyone else in town. It's fucking insane to stand behind that bar on a Thursday night, and it's an experience not many are lucky enough to experience. I can sell any beer to any person, I can make a cocktail that will make new friends, and if you want a french win to pair with your god damn chicken wings, I can do it. I studied pretty damn hard to get here. It kind of sucks when I tell people I'm a bar tender and they imagine I stand around all day drinking and pouring beers, I'm pretty insulted. But that's something I think a lot of bartenders deal with.

I've always felt like "mixologist" is a term that asks for respect. I think everyone that works behind the bar would like respect and we don't always get it from our customers. But I'd like to think we should always be able to find respect in our own community, in a common understanding of what makes this job challenging and fulfilling. The term mixologist has always seemed like a way to disrespect other bartenders. When people ask me if I'm a mixologist, I usually say "I'm just a guy that spills liquor into cups." Which helps keep some of my ingredients a secret. "what is that?" "I don't know, I found it in the kitchen yesterday."

But this is a description of my opinion, not fact. I have nothing against you personally, it sounds like you're great at making cocktails. Personally, I will never associate with the word "mixologist" because of what it means to me.

As an aside, you can study beer, take tests and become a Master Cicerone or take the BJCP, you can study wine [and whiskey and cigars], take a [very] rigorous course, and become a sommelier. But there isn't really any kind of test for people who make cocktails, unless you've won a respected competition. There's the WSET, but how many people have even heard of that, will take that, and what does it really mean for your ability to tend bar or even to mix cocktails?

As another aside, for every experience I've had with a person that describes themself as a mixologist, I have been standing behind my bar. It is an encounter similar to when someone describes themself as a "beer expert," asks for Pliny the Younger off of schedule, and is outraged when [of fucking course], we don't have it. There is an association between the phrase "I am a mixologist," and 'I don't follow the golden rule when I go out drinking.'

I take part in a mock government program where we debate bills and propositions that we make. This is mainly done for fun, but it is also very educational. One of the bills I made was to legalize prostitution in the state that I currently reside in. I was widely supported outside of the official debate, but once it was time to decide if the bill went on it was shot down 7-5. I am curious on your opinions on the topic.

 

If anyone is interested here is the bill:

  • AN ACT TO: Legalize the action of Prostitution

  • SECTION I - Prostitution has been around for thousands of years, and for as long as prostitution has been around society has been fighting it. This proposal will legalize the act of prostitution in brothels and through escort services, but keeping street prostitution illegal. On average a prostitute makes about 100,000 US dollars in a year, but most of this money is extorted from them in return for security. This proposal will restrict the amount of money security providers will be able to charge an individual prostitute, thus ensuring prostitutes keep their hard earned money. The state will be able to collect income tax from the prostitutes. With the average amount of prostitutes per state (20 thousand) and the amount of money made on average, Louisiana would make about 128 million dollars a year in tax revenue. This proposal will keep prostitution off our streets, away from our children, and help boost a new industry to thrive.

  • SECTION II - This law will require each business that wishes to offer the option of prostitution to register as a prostitution business, acquire a license enabling them to provide the service, to require each prostitute to use a condom during any sexual act, and to restrict anyone under the age of 18 from entering their place of business (If alcohol is offered then the required age to enter would be 21). Each prostitute will be required to register as a prostitute with the Louisiana State Prostitution Association (L.S.P.A.) and update their registration yearly. Each prostitute will be required to have a STD check-up every ten days to limit the spread of venereal disease. If their results are positive then they will be required to take the appropriate treatment options within 10 days of receiving their results; if there are no treatment options they will be required to warn each customer before the acts are committed. Anyone providing security for the prostitutes will not be allowed to charge more than 10% of their client’s annual salary: contracts will have to be updated annually. Each business offering this service will be required to have an inspection each fiscal quarter by the L.S.P.A. in order to make sure each business is running smoothly and is up to code. After the first five years of the business operation they will only be required to have two inspections per year. If this law is passed it will take effect on January 1, 2016. Each business and prostitute will be able to begin registering three months in advance.

  • SECTION III - Over time this bill will be able to support itself through the taxes on the businesses and prostitutes, but in the beginning the program will need about 1,000,000 US dollars to start. This money would come from the Louisiana State surplus, which in 2014 there was over 100 million dollars.

  • SECTION IV - The preexisting laws for street prostitution and prostitution with a minor will remain. If a business offering the service of prostitution is not following the required laws the first offence will be a 10,000 dollar fine, the second offence will be a 35,000 dollar fine and or 6 months in jail, and the third offence will be a 50,000 dollar fine, 24 months in jail, and the business’ operations will cease. If prostitutes are not following the required laws they will be charged with the same penalties as street prostitution. People who participate in illegal prostitution will get 6 months in jail and or a 250 dollar fine.

Something like "digital currency" is much more neutral and tells people what it is right away.
